newsitem.title: INDIA: Confusion over death toll in India train blast.
newsitem.headline: Confusion over death toll in India train blast.

text.p: Two days after suspected tribal militants attacked a crowded passenger train in northeastern India, there was still confusion over how many people were killed.
Local officials insisted on Wednesday that 33 people died in Monday evening's attack on the Brahmaputra Mail express train.
But witnesses said some bodies had not been accounted for, and army officers said the death toll was far higher.

Initially, senior police officials feared the twin bomb explosions killed as many as 300 passengers. The figure was based on early reports that the blast had completely destroyed three carriages, each one carrying about 100 passengers.
But after rescuers reached the site of the attack near Kokrajhar, 200 km (125 miles) west of Assam state's largest city Guwahati, officials dramatically reduced the toll.
S. Thadou, a senior administrator in the Kokrajhar district administration, told Reuters on Wednesday that there were 33 dead and 63 injured, including 22 seriously.

But witnesses said some bodies were removed before the official rescue operation got under way in the remote part of Assam state, where an ethnic insurgency has added to problems posed by poor transport and telecommunications links.
Some survivors took away injured, dead and dying before the first police and medics reached the site, residents said.
One witness saw three bodies being carried away.
"I saw four labourers carrying three dead bodies, including one child, on a stretcher through the fields close to the wrecked train," a local reporter said.
In rural sections of India, relatives often do not register deaths. Some corpses may have been abandoned by residents who did not want to deal with the bureaucracy of reporting a death.
One local official who asked not to be named said about 60 people were believed to have died. A senior military officer told Reuters up to 150 people may have perished.
The search for bodies continued through Wednesday but no more were found, said divisional railway manager Asit Gupta, responsible for coordinating relief operations.
The main rescue effort was delayed by the remoteness of the site chosen by the attackers, believed to be Bodo tribal extremists fighting for a separate homeland.
The attack occurred seven km (four miles) outside Kokrajhar and four km (2.5 miles) from the next station Fakiragram.
But the only way to reach the site by road led through farmland thick with members of the Bodoland Liberation Tigers Force (BLTF), Thadou said.
Rescuers had to cross a 100 metre (yard) long bamboo bridge which cannot support heavy vehicles. The road ends in the middle of farmland, leaving rescuers with a two-km (one mile) walk.
The first help party, led by Thadou, reached the site three hours after the explosion and was unable to offer much substantial aid because of the darkness.
Two hours later an emergency railway and medical team arrived with an armed escort equipped with kerosene lamps.
